lessons.title: The coming of the Germans: the treaty of 1884
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 3 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Explain why Germany became interested in Kamerun
Describe the Germano-Duala treaty of July 1884
Explain the reactions of the Duala and rival powers
Explain how Kamerun became a German protectorate
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: date and signatories of the 1884 treaty, the arrival of the British consul after the treaty, the names of firms, and how the treaty is explained in the syllabus; the interpretation of the treaty is debated.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: By the early 1880s German firms such as **Woermann** and **Jantzen and Thormählen** were trading on the coast. They wanted the German government to protect their trade. Germany, newly united (in 1871) and growing in industry, also wanted **raw materials**, **markets** and a place among the great powers. The German Chancellor agreed to take **protectorates** in Africa, and **Gustav Nachtigal** was sent to the coast.

blocks.caption: From the treaty to 1916
blocks.alt: A timeline from 1870 to 1920 with 1871, 1884, 1914, 1916 and the period of German rule.

blocks.title: The treaty of 12 July 1884
blocks.md: On **12 July 1884** Duala chiefs, among them the leaders usually named **Bell** and **Akwa**, signed a treaty with representatives of the German firms and government. By it the Duala leaders handed over powers of **government and the right to make laws** along the Wouri area, while keeping some rights, such as their lands, their customs and their trade. German flags were raised, and **Kamerun** became a German protectorate.

The British had earlier received requests from some coastal chiefs for protection but had delayed. When a British consul arrived a few days after the treaty, **Germany was already in control** of the Wouri area. A **Berlin conference** (1884–85) soon agreed rules for the scramble for Africa. In the following years, Germany extended control inland by treaties and military expeditions, and the borders of Kamerun were settled by agreements with Britain and France.

blocks.title: Why the Duala signed
blocks.md: Some chiefs hoped for **protection** and for a stronger position over rivals; they wanted to keep their role in the trade; and they believed the treaty left their land and customs untouched. Later the Duala complained that Germany did not respect these promises. Historians still discuss how the treaty was understood by the two sides.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
blocks.md:
- Kamerun was a German protectorate, then later divided; the name 'Cameroon' is from Portuguese, not German.
- The Duala signed a treaty, but the Germans later expanded far beyond the Duala area; the treaty did not give them all of Cameroon.
- The treaty date is 12 July 1884, not 1914.

blocks.title: Example 1: motives
blocks.statement: Give two reasons why Germany wanted colonies in Kamerun.
steps: German firms wanted protection for their trade.
The country wanted raw materials, markets and prestige.
So trade protection and economic and political motives.
blocks.answer: Protection of trade; raw materials and markets (and prestige).

blocks.title: Example 2: what the Duala kept
blocks.statement: Name two things the Duala leaders wanted to keep under the treaty.
steps: They wanted to keep ownership of their land.
They also wished to keep their customs and their trade.
These were written as conditions in the treaty.

lessons.title: German administration, economy and resistance
lessons.programRef: Cameroon anglophone secondary History syllabus, Form 3 — to be checked against the official text
lessons.author: CastBridge (AI draft)
lessons.source: Original writing following the Cameroonian curriculum; to be reviewed by a teacher
objectives: Describe the economic development under Germany
reviewNotes: Teacher to verify: capital moved to Buea in 1901, the 1911 treaty and Neukamerun, railway status (Northern line to Nkongsamba, Central line begun), the 1913–14 events and the execution date of Manga Bell (August 1914), and the balance of the evaluation.

Draft for teacher review: only well-established facts are used and the tone is neutral; every date and name must be verified against the official History syllabus and standard references before release.

blocks.md: Kamerun was governed by a **governor**, assisted by officials, a police force and soldiers (the *Schutztruppe*). The capital was first at Douala and later at **Buea** (from 1901) on the slopes of Mount Cameroon. The country was divided into districts under German officers. Germany used **chiefs** as local agents in some areas, but Germans controlled land, labour and taxes. A treaty with France in **1911** added extra territory (called *Neukamerun*).

blocks.caption: Two sides of German rule
blocks.alt: Two columns listing developments and hardships under German rule.

blocks.title: Economy
blocks.md: Germany developed **plantations** (cocoa, bananas, rubber, oil palm, tobacco) around Mount Cameroon and the coast, and **railways** and **roads** to move goods to the port of Douala: the **Northern Railway** towards Nkongsamba was completed and the **Central Railway** towards Yaoundé was begun. Africans were required to pay **taxes** and to give **labour** for plantations and railways, often under harsh conditions.

blocks.title: Social change
blocks.md: Missions (Basel, Baptist, Catholic and others) and the government opened **schools**, often teaching in German or local languages, and built **clinics**. Education trained clerks, teachers and craftworkers. Many Africans were forced off their land to make room for plantations, and heavy labour, punishments and disease caused hardship.

**Resistance.** Many peoples resisted German expansion: for example the Bakweri at Buea in the 1890s, the Bulu and Maka in the south and east, and Fulani and other leaders in the north. The best known case is the **Duala resistance of 1913–14**, led by **Rudolf Douala Manga Bell**, who opposed plans to move the Duala from their homes on the riverbank. He was arrested and **executed in August 1914**. The Bamum kingdom under King Njoya kept relatively good relations with Germany.

blocks.title: Be careful
blocks.md:
- Evaluate German rule fairly: it brought roads, railways and schools but also forced labour, loss of land and violence.
- Resistance took many forms: armed battles, refusing work, writing petitions, and flight.
- Avoid using words such as 'good' or 'bad' alone; give evidence for each point.

blocks.title: Example 1: effect of plantations
blocks.statement: Give one benefit and one cost of plantations in Kamerun.
steps: Plantations created export crops and paid some wages.
But they took land from farmers and used forced labour.
So a benefit is export income and a cost is loss of land.
blocks.answer: Benefit: exports/wages; cost: loss of land and forced labour.

blocks.title: Example 2: resistance
blocks.statement: Why did the Duala resist in 1913–14?
steps: Germany planned to move them from the river bank.
They wanted to keep their homes and land.
So they protested and sent petitions.
blocks.answer: To keep their land and homes.
